operationalization: Fit 3D or 2D outlines of unilocular foraminiferal tests (such as Orbulina and Lagena) to constant-mean-curvature fluid-drop profiles (sphere, pendant/sessile drop, catenoid/unduloid necks) and test whether residuals are smaller than under unconstrained geometric or cytoskeletal-templated models.

candidate_datasets.name: Foraminifera.eu Project
candidate_datasets.role: Provides thousands of SEM and light-microscope images of unilocular foraminiferal tests across Lagena, Orbulina, and related genera for outline extraction and curvature fitting.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Hosts 3D micro-CT scans of foraminiferal tests that allow direct measurement of principal curvatures across the test surface.

obstacles: Morphological fit to a constant-mean-curvature surface tests the geometric prediction of surface tension, but direct measurements of cytoplasmic interfacial tension during biomineralization are not available in public datasets.
Costae, spines, and complex apertural necks in many Lagena species depart from simple isotropic fluid-drop equilibria.
rationale: The geometric consequence of Thompson's claim—that single-chambered tests follow constant-mean-curvature surfaces—can be tested directly using existing micrograph and micro-CT collections. However, because static test morphology alone cannot fully separate passive fluid surface tension from active cytoskeletal scaffolding during chamber formation, existing data only partially resolve the mechanistic claim.

operationalization: Compare chamber addition trajectories across multilocular Foraminifera and Radiolaria in 3D morphological datasets to test whether external, asymmetric accretion of rigid chambers is a necessary and sufficient predictor of spiral coiling versus concentric or rectilinear growth.

candidate_datasets.name: Foraminifera.eu Project
candidate_datasets.role: Documents multilocular foraminiferal growth geometries across spiral, uniserial, biserial, and annular taxa.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Contains 3D micro-CT reconstructions of internal chamber sequences in multilocular Foraminifera.

obstacles: External accretion of rigid increments produces rectilinear (Nodosaria), annular (Orbitolites), and milioline forms just as readily unless an asymmetry in placement is also specified.
The claim states a general physical tendency rather than a sharp quantitative threshold.
rationale: Existing morphological catalogs of Foraminifera and Radiolaria clearly document which taxa grow by external rigid chamber addition and which adopt spiral versus concentric or rectilinear forms. However, because external accretion alone produces both spiral and non-spiral shells depending on aperture position, the claim is only partially resolvable as stated.

operationalization: Measure the sign of mean curvature (convex versus concave toward the aperture/growth direction) and fit minimal-surface / constant-mean-curvature equations to 3D micro-CT reconstructions of foraminiferal and Nautilus septa.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Provides 3D micro-CT datasets of Nautilus pompilius shells and chambered foraminiferal tests for quantifying septal curvature and surface area.

obstacles: Ammonoid and complex foraminiferal septa exhibit fluted or folded margins that deviate from simple minimal surfaces under hydrostatic pressure alone.
Direct in vivo pressure differentials during septal secretion are not recorded in morphological scan archives.
rationale: The geometric core of the claim—opposite direction of septal convexity in Foraminifera versus Nautilus and approximation to a surface of minimal area given boundary constraints—is directly measurable on 3D micro-CT scans already available in public repositories. While pressure during secretion is inferred rather than directly measured in museum specimens, the morphological prediction is crisp and testable now.

operationalization: Fit polar radius versus whorl angle r(theta) = a * exp(b * theta) to axial and equatorial sections or 3D micro-CT ontogenetic series of spiral Foraminifera, and test self-similarity across growth stages against Archimedean or allometric power-law rivals.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Hosts 3D micro-CT scans of planispiral and trochospiral Foraminifera enabling chamber-by-chamber ontogenetic shape comparison.

candidate_datasets.name: Foraminifera.eu Project
candidate_datasets.role: Provides equatorial cross-sections and oriented images of spiral foraminiferal tests across diverse families.

obstacles: Many foraminiferal species show ontogenetic changes in coiling rate between juvenile (proloculus/neanic) and adult or gerontic stages.
rationale: Testing whether spiral foraminiferal shells follow a logarithmic spiral and maintain geometric self-similarity across ontogeny is a straightforward morphometric analysis. High-resolution cross-sections and micro-CT scans of chambered Foraminifera are publicly available and allow clean discrimination between logarithmic spirals and non-self-similar growth trajectories.

operationalization: Measure successive whorl breadths (radii or heights per revolution) in axial and sagittal thin sections of Fusulina species, compute the ratio r_{n+1}/r_n and corresponding tangential spiral angle, and test whether the mean ratio is approximately 1.5 (angle ~86°) and constant across whorls.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Catalogs occurrences, taxonomic metadata, and linked morphological measurements of Pennsylvanian-Permian fusulinid Foraminifera.

candidate_datasets.name: Foraminifera.eu Project
candidate_datasets.role: Contains thin-section micrographs of Fusulina and allied fusulinids suitable for direct whorl-breadth measurement.

obstacles: Whorl expansion rates in fusulinids often shift between the inner juvenarium and outer mature volutions.
rationale: This is a highly specific quantitative claim about whorl breadth ratios and spiral angle in Fusulina. Fusulinid biostratigraphy relies routinely on oriented thin-section measurements of volution height and radius across whorls, so existing public thin-section archives and published measurement tables can confirm or refute the 1:1.5 ratio directly.

operationalization: Using 3D micro-CT reconstructions of chambered Foraminifera, measure individual chamber volumes V_k and cumulative test volume sum_{i=1}^{k-1} V_i, and test whether V_k is linearly proportional to cumulative prior volume (producing a constant ratio V_{k+1}/V_k).

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Provides volumetric 3D micro-CT segmentations of successive chambers in benthic and planktonic Foraminifera.

obstacles: Test chamber volume is a proxy for cytoplasmic mass at the time of chamber formation, which may not fill all prior chambers uniformly.
Chamber volumes often exhibit episodic fluctuations related to environmental stress or gametogenesis.
rationale: Three-dimensional micro-CT segmentation of foraminiferal chambers is an established technique with open datasets on MorphoSource. Because the claim links exponential chamber volume scaling (V_{k+1}/V_k = const) to growth proportional to cumulative volume, one can directly test both the constancy of successive chamber volume ratios and the proportionality of new chamber volume to cumulative preceding volume.

operationalization: Simulate chamber addition on 3D micro-CT geometries of foraminiferal shells by minimizing surface area of each new chamber of volume V_k = c * V_{k-1} wetting the existing test, and compare the predicted contact angles and spiral paths against Rhumbler's constant-contact-angle rule and actual chamber geometries.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Supplies 3D chamber geometries and suture contact angles across ontogeny in spiral Foraminifera.

obstacles: Minimal surface area and constant contact angle are mathematically coupled for wetting droplets via Young's equation, making it difficult to cleanly separate Thompson's formulation from Rhumbler's using static geometry alone.
Actual chamber morphogenesis involves pseudopodial templates rather than passive liquid drops.
rationale: One can test the geometric predictions of surface-area minimization plus proportional volume growth on 3D micro-CT scans of foraminiferal tests. However, because constant contact angles and surface energy minimization are physically equivalent for homogeneous wetting drops, static morphological data only partially discriminate Thompson's broad principle from Rhumbler's specific contact-angle formulation.

operationalization: Classify spiral Foraminifera by habitat/life mode (epiphytic/epilithic attached benthic, free-living benthic, planktonic) and quantify spire height-to-diameter ratio (planispiral vs trochospiral/helicoid) and umbilical/spiral side flattening across species.

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS)
candidate_datasets.role: Provides taxonomic classifications and ecological/functional group annotations (benthic vs planktonic) for extant Foraminifera.

candidate_datasets.name: Foraminifera.eu Project
candidate_datasets.role: Provides lateral, umbilical, and spiral view images of benthic (Rotalia, Cibicides, Discorbis) and planktonic (Globigerina) species for measuring spire height and ventral flattening.

obstacles: Many attached benthic Foraminifera (such as Cibicides and Discorbina) are low-trochospiral with one flattened attachment side rather than strictly planispiral, requiring careful separation of discoid flattening from strict bilateral planispirality.
rationale: The comparative morphological correlation between attached benthic habit, flattened umbilical/attachment surfaces, and low/discoid coiling versus globose helicoid spires in planktonic forms (Globigerina) can be tested immediately using existing taxonomic, ecological, and imaging databases.

operationalization: Compare SSU rDNA molecular phylogenies and single-specimen barcoding against traditional morphospecies and morphogenera in Peneroplis and other variable Foraminifera to test whether distinct named morphospecies/genera share identical or conspecific genotypes.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Contains extensive foraminiferal SSU rDNA sequences linked to voucher morphotypes, including Peneroplis and soritid species.

candidate_datasets.name: PR2 (Protist Ribosomal Reference database)
candidate_datasets.role: Curates 18S rRNA sequences of Foraminifera and other protists for assessing genetic divergence among morphological taxa.

obstacles: Genetic barcoding has sequenced only a fraction of described foraminiferal morphospecies, and in many groups cryptic genetic species outnumber morphospecies rather than the reverse.
rationale: Thompson's hypothesis that many named foraminiferal species and genera (especially in Peneroplis) are ecophenotypic or developmental variants of the same organism is directly testable today by pairing morphological classifications with public SSU rDNA sequence databases. Existing molecular studies in GenBank allow testing whether divergent shell morphotypes belong to a single genetic species or represent distinct clades.

operationalization: Test whether foraminiferal shell morphotypes evolve neutrally without differential extinction rates, environmental niche sorting, or directional selection across Cretaceous-to-Recent stratigraphic time series.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Provides stratigraphic ranges and extinction/origination histories of foraminiferal genera from the Cretaceous to the Recent.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF)
candidate_datasets.role: Supplies global Cenozoic and modern foraminiferal occurrence records across environmental gradients.

obstacles: The claim that 'none is fitter or less fit to survive than another' is a sweeping conceptual negation of selection across all environments and traits.
Inferring neutral fitness versus adaptive selection from fossil longevity and diversity distributions is confounded by taxonomic lumping and environmental turnover.
rationale: While Thompson's claim is framed conceptually, its empirical implication—that foraminiferal shell forms have equal survival fitness and show neutral persistence since the Cretaceous—can be partially tested against paleontological extinction, iterative evolution, and environmental sorting records. Because fossil range data show strong differential extinction by morphotype (e.g., at the K-Pg boundary) and strong depth/temperature niche sorting, existing data can partially test and challenge the claim, though fitness equivalence is hard to operationalize cleanly.

operationalization: Map discrete shell architectures (e.g., uniserial, biserial, planispiral, trochospiral, keeled globorotaliid) onto molecular and stratophenetic phylogenies of Foraminifera to test for statistically significant convergent (homoplastic) origins of identical morphotypes across independent lineages.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Provides multi-gene and SSU rDNA sequences across major foraminiferal orders demonstrating polyphyly of traditional chamber-arrangement morphogroups.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Documents iterative homeomorphy in planktonic and benthic Foraminifera across Mesozoic and Cenozoic radiations.

obstacles: What counts as an 'identical form' depends on the morphological resolution chosen (overall chamber arrangement vs fine wall ultrastructure).
rationale: Both molecular phylogenetics of extant Foraminifera (which revealed widespread polyphyly of morphogenera defined by chamber arrangement) and the Cenozoic fossil record of iterative homeomorphs provide direct, public data to test whether identical shell forms have evolved independently multiple times.

operationalization: Evaluate the incidence of repaired shell breakage (sublethal damage) and intact versus fragmented test proportions across foraminiferal assemblages from varying hydrodynamic and predatory regimes.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Hosts marine sediment core datasets reporting foraminiferal fragmentation indices, test preservation, and assemblage compositions.

obstacles: Fragmentation in sediment cores mixes post-mortem taphonomic dissolution and mechanical breakage with in vivo lethal or sublethal breakage.
Demonstrating that strength is or is not a selective advantage requires linking test mechanics to in vivo survival fitness.
rationale: Marine micropaleontological datasets in PANGAEA routinely record test fragmentation and preservation indices, and studies of sublethal test repair document that living Foraminifera do experience mechanical damage. However, separating post-mortem taphonomic breakage from selective mortality in living populations is only partially achievable with existing open datasets.

operationalization: Test whether the abundance and size distribution of dead foraminiferal tests across marine sediment grain-size fractions correlate with hydraulic settling velocity equivalence (Shields parameter / settling speed matching host quartz grains) rather than living habitat avoidance.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Contains paired marine surface-sediment grain-size distributions, current velocities, and living (Rose Bengal stained) versus dead foraminiferal assemblage counts.

obstacles: Epiphytic or epilithic taxa attached to coarse substrates while alive may be winnowed away only after death.
rationale: Paired datasets of sediment granulometry and stained (living) versus unstained (dead) foraminiferal assemblages in PANGAEA directly test Thompson's hydraulic sorting mechanism. Comparing living occurrences on coarse substrates with post-mortem size sorting across muds and sands cleanly discriminates hydraulic winnowing from active habitat avoidance.

operationalization: Measure the congruence (e.g., Robinson-Foulds distance or phylogenetic signal of shell geometric parameters) between traditional morphology-based classifications of Foraminifera and independent molecular phylogenies.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Supplies molecular sequence data across Foraminifera to compare genetic clades against classical morphology-based families and genera.

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS)
candidate_datasets.role: Records the taxonomic hierarchy of Foraminifera, including revisions where molecular phylogenies overturned purely morphological groupings.

obstacles: The second half of the claim is methodological and normative ('compelled to revise the vague canons which connect classification with phylogeny'), though its empirical premise of widespread homoplasy in physically constrained forms is testable.
rationale: While framed as a conceptual warning about phylogenetic inference, the empirical core—that simple geometric shell characters in Foraminifera are poor indicators of consanguinity compared to independent phylogenetic markers—has been directly tested by comparing morphological classifications with molecular phylogenies in GenBank. Because the claim blends an empirical prediction of homoplasy with a methodological prescription, it is scored as partially resolvable.

operationalization: Extract the median centerline and anterior/posterior surface curves from 3D scans of rhinoceros horns, test for zero lateral torsion (planarity) and fit a planar logarithmic spiral r(theta) = a * exp(b * theta) against circular-arc or power-law alternatives.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Contains 3D CT and surface scans of rhinoceros skulls and keratin horns across extant species.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Provides CT scans of vertebrate cranial and horn structures including rhinoceroses.

obstacles: Rhinoceros horns suffer substantial anterior tip wear and rubbing in life, which truncates and alters the distal spiral profile.
Direct measurement of anterior versus posterior keratin proliferation rates is less widely archived than static 3D horn geometry and growth rings.
rationale: Three-dimensional scans and lateral radiographs of rhinoceros horns in public morphology repositories allow direct testing of planarity and logarithmic spiral curvature, as well as measuring anterior-to-posterior spacing of annual growth increments along the horn.

operationalization: Reflect the 3D centerline and surface mesh of the left horn across the cranial sagittal plane and compute the Procrustes or root-mean-square deviation from the right horn, testing whether torsion signs are opposite and curvature/spiral parameters are equal across Bovid species.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Hosts 3D surface and CT scans of bovid crania with paired horns across sheep, goats, oxen, and antelopes.

candidate_datasets.name: Phenome10K
candidate_datasets.role: Provides 3D cranial scans of ruminant artiodactyls for bilateral symmetry and enantiomorphic spiral comparison.

obstacles: Fluctuating asymmetry and mechanical damage during combat introduce minor individual deviations from exact mirror symmetry.
rationale: Whether paired bovid horns are enantiomorphic (mirror-image conjugate spirals with opposite chirality) is a pure geometric property that can be tested rapidly and decisively on existing 3D skull and horn scans in MorphoSource and Phenome10K.

operationalization: Fit 3D logarithmic spiral/helical equations to the horn centerline and measure the ratio of outer-to-inner longitudinal horn growth-ring increments along the horn length across bovid species.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Provides 3D CT and surface meshes of bovid horns across dozens of species, capturing both overall spiral geometry and external annual growth annuli.

obstacles: In many bovid species, seasonal or age-related shifts in horn growth rates slightly alter the curvature ratio between juvenile and adult segments.
rationale: Both the geometric shape of the horn (continuous logarithmic spiral) and its generative growth increments (visible externally as annual horn rings whose widths on opposite sides record longitudinal growth rates) are preserved on bovid horn specimens available in 3D scan repositories.

operationalization: Estimate the constant tangential spiral angle from 3D scans and calibrated osteological photographs of Oryx, Capra (including Capra aegagrus/ibex), Ovis ammon, and domestic Scottish Blackface/Highland rams, and test whether they follow the predicted ranking and numerical values (<40°, <70°, ~75°, >75°).

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Provides 3D cranium and horn scans of Oryx, Capra, and Ovis species for direct spiral angle measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF)
candidate_datasets.role: Aggregates natural history museum specimen records with calibrated dorsal/lateral cranial and horn photographs of Bovidae.

obstacles: Projection of 3D space curves onto a plane alters the apparent 2D spiral angle unless computed consistently in 3D or along the principal plane of curvature.
rationale: Thompson gives explicit numerical spiral-angle bounds for specific bovid taxa (Oryx, Capra, Ovis ammon, Highland ram). Museum 3D scans and calibrated specimen images of these genera exist in open repositories and allow direct verification of both the homologous spiral fit and the specific angular progression.

operationalization: Fit 3D equiangular helices (cone/helical shear angle plus planar logarithmic spiral angle) to horn scans and museum images of argali subspecies/species (Ovis ammon ammon, O. a. polii, O. a. hodgsoni) and test whether inter-taxon variance lies primarily in the axial shearing/torsion parameter rather than the planar spiral angle.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Hosts 3D scans of Ovis ammon and related caprine horns for 3D spiral and helical parameter extraction.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF)
candidate_datasets.role: Provides digitized museum horn specimens and photographs of Central Asian Ovis ammon populations (Marco Polo, Tibetan, and Altai argali).

obstacles: 3D scans of all three specific geographic forms of Ovis ammon have modest sample sizes in open 3D archives, though supplemented by extensive museum photography.
rationale: Decomposing a 3D horn curve into its planar logarithmic spiral angle and its axial shearing (helical pitch) component is standard in theoretical morphology (e.g., Raup/Skalak models). Existing museum scans and digitized collections of Ovis ammon subspecies allow testing whether the planar spiral constant is conserved while helical shear diverges.

operationalization: Measure growth-ring width around the circumference of successive horn annuli in 3D scans of planispiral versus helicoid ruminant horns to determine the angular separation between the loci of maximum and minimum longitudinal growth, and correlate its departure from 180° with the horn's helical torsion.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Provides 3D surface scans of bovid horns showing circumferential growth annuli and 3D centerline torsion.

obstacles: Annual growth rings can be worn or indistinct in smooth-horned bovids, restricting measurements to taxa with prominent transverse ridges (Capra, Ovis, Oryx, Hippotragus).
rationale: Mathematically, the statement is a kinematic theorem of space curves; empirically, because bovid horns preserve transverse periodic growth rings around their circumference, the angular positions of maximal and minimal longitudinal increment can be measured directly on 3D surface meshes and tested against the horn's helical torsion.

operationalization: Measure differential shear stress, collagenous attachment density, and keratin sliding rates at the interface between the bony horncore periosteum and germinative horn sheath around the circumference during active horn growth, and test whether mechanical retardation accounts for curvature independently of basal keratinocyte proliferation rates.
obstacles: No publicly available datasets measure in vivo circumferential adhesion mechanics or differential sliding between the unsolidified keratin sheath and bony horncore across ruminant species.

As Thompson himself notes, differential basal proliferation and differential adhesive retardation produce identical external horn geometry, so static osteological/horn scans cannot discriminate between them.
rationale: Because Thompson explicitly points out that unequal adhesive retardation and unequal initial growth rates yield the exact same external spiral curve, static museum scans cannot distinguish the two mechanisms. Resolving whether horncore-sheath adhesion is a primary causal factor requires histological and biomechanical measurements of the living horncore-sheath interface that do not exist in public datasets.

operationalization: Across species of Bovidae (antelopes, goats, sheep), regress mean spiral curvature (normalized by horn length or basal radius) against basal horn cross-sectional thickness/diameter using 3D cranial scans and comparative morphometric datasets.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Provides 3D scans of bovid horns across a wide range of basal thicknesses and curvatures.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web (ADW)
candidate_datasets.role: Contains comparative cranial photographs and morphological descriptions across Bovidae.

obstacles: Curvature has units of inverse length, so the correlation depends on whether raw curvature, radius of curvature, or spiral angle (dimensionless) is tested against horn thickness.
rationale: Testing the interspecific correlation between horn basal thickness and spiral curvature across antelopes, goats, and sheep requires only standard morphometric measurements from widely available 3D museum scans.

operationalization: Digitize the 3D trajectories of transverse growth rings and cross-sectional contours on high-resolution surface scans of non-circular helicoid horns (Ovis, Capra, twisted antelopes) versus circular ox horns (Bos), and compare the axial warping profile of the growth rings against Saint-Venant's warping function for torsion of a prism of the measured cross-section.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Hosts high-resolution 3D surface meshes of sheep, goat, antelope, and cattle horns showing cross-sectional shapes and transverse growth annuli.

obstacles: Sinuous growth lines could also arise from spatially periodic variation in basal keratin proliferation around the non-circular germinal ring rather than elastic/plastic Saint-Venant warping after secretion.
rationale: The geometric prediction—that growth rings are planar on circular/non-torsional horns (oxen) and follow Saint-Venant's cross-sectional warping curve (inflexions on the faces, extrema at the corners) on non-circular twisted horns—can be tested directly using 3D surface scans of bovid horns.
